_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: “You shall not curse the deaf”: this implies both an ordinary curse and a curse using the Name, for the prohibition stands on it; and the verse “that you may fear the Name” comes to teach us that he is flogged, as it says: “Then the Lord will make your plagues wondrous.” Another explanation: you cannot say that he is not atoned for by lashes alone, for he certainly is atoned for by lashes alone. For it is written: “You shall not curse the deaf,” and in Sanhedrin, in the chapter Arba Mitot (Sanhedrin 66a), we derive a verbal analogy from this prohibition, written about the helpless, such as “You shall not curse the deaf,” the lowest of them all, and what is written about a prince: “And a prince among your people you shall not curse” [Exodus 22:27]. Just as there there is only lashes alone, so too for the helpless lashes alone suffice. And there they establish it as one who curses using the Name, since it is derived from one who curses his father, about whom it is written “when he pronounces the Name” [Leviticus 24:16]. Therefore you cannot say that lashes do not suffice for him. [I have this] not from my teacher, but from Rabbi Yitzḥak son of Rabbi Menaḥem, of blessed memory. [On this second explanation, “you cannot say” answers the objection at the end of 3b that lashes alone should not suffice.]
rashi:a1.2: And if you wish, say [Rashi’s text has these words, which are not in our printed Gemara]: that is, this verse “that you may fear the Name” comes for one who curses another using the Name, for we do not find that the Torah punishes unless it has warned.
rashi:a1.3: Granted, if you say: that that verse comes for one who curses another using the Name, and its warning is from what is written, “You shall not curse the deaf,” which is established as one who curses another using the Name, as I explained above. Therefore it is written here: “If you will not observe to do” and so on, that is, that you curse your fellow using the Name, about which you were warned; “then the Lord will make wondrous” and so on, that he is liable to lashes.
rashi:a1.4: From where is its warning: that is, we have found the punishment, “then the Lord will make wondrous” and so on. From where is the warning, that the verse warned not to pronounce the name of Heaven in vain?
rashi:a2.1: Why not: in astonishment. [Is it so] that we do not find that the Torah warned against pronouncing His name in vain? But here [in “You shall fear the Lord your God”] it warned, and there it punished, “then the Lord will make wondrous” and so on, and the mention of the Name is written in “If you will not observe to do” and so on. So the verse can still be established as one who pronounces the name of Heaven in vain.
rashi:a2.2: That is a warning stated as a positive mitzva: and that is not called a warning. Therefore “that you may fear the glorious Name” is established as one who curses another using the Name, for whom we find a warning stated as a prohibition, “You shall not curse the deaf”; and it is not established as one who pronounces the name of Heaven in vain, for whom we find no warning stated as a prohibition. [On the next passage:] The Gemara goes back to what was said above, where Rabbi Yosei said: Also one who separates teruma before first fruits is flogged.
tosafot:a1.1: You cannot say, as it is written “You shall not curse the deaf”: since we have found a warning for one who curses, we should establish this verse of lashes as one who curses another using the Name, rather than as one who pronounces the name of Heaven in vain, for which we have found no explicit warning.
gershom:a1.1: You cannot say that lashes would not suffice for him, for it is written: “You shall not curse the deaf.” Evidently it carries only a prohibition, and this “vehifla” comes to make him liable to lashes.
gershom:a2.1: If you wish, say: it is certainly reasonable that this “that you may fear” refers to one who curses another using the Name.
gershom:a3.1: For granted, one who curses another using the Name, its warning, and so on. [The Gemara objects:] Derive it from “You shall fear the Lord your God,” and that is the warning not to pronounce the name of Heaven in vain.
gershom:a4.1: That: “You shall fear” is a warning stated as a positive mitzva, and one is not flogged for it.
rashi:a3.1: These are first fruits: first fruits are called “fullness” because as soon as the grain has become full and its work is completed, it is fixed for first fruits.
rashi:a3.2: This is teruma: since it makes a mixture [medama’at, when it falls into non-sacred produce] and is nullified only in one hundred and one, the verse expresses it with the word for mixture [dema]. And the Merciful One says: You shall not put the fullness after the mixture, for at the outset he should have brought the fullness, that is, the first fruits; and if he puts it later, he is flogged.
tosafot:a3.1: “Your fullness”: these are first fruits. Rashi explained: it is called fullness because as soon as the grain is heaped up and its work is completed it is fixed for first fruits; and “your outflow [dima’akha]”: this is teruma, because it makes a mixture and is nullified [in one hundred and one], the verse expresses it with the word for mixture (Rashi’s words). This is not convincing, for that [ratio] is only rabbinic. Rabbi Moshe of Pontoise explained that teruma is called dema [liquid] because it applies to liquids, while first fruits apply only to solids, since first fruits are brought only from fruit, as stated in the chapter HaOr VehaRotev (Ḥullin 120b): “Fruit you bring, but you do not bring a beverage.”
gershom:a5.1: And it is taught (in the Sifrei) [in the Mekhilta]: “Your fullness”: these are the first fruits, which are taken from the full produce, that is, at the beginning, while everything is still full and nothing has yet been taken from it.
gershom:a6.1: “And your outflow [dima’akha]”: this is teruma, which is taken from the mixture, since in them there is the non-sacred produce of the first fruits together with the untithed produce of the teruma. And we also say in the Sifra: Let first fruits come before [teruma], for they are called by four names [first fruits, reishit, teruma and dema; first fruits are called teruma, as it is written: “the teruma of your hand,” these are the first fruits; and teruma is called dema. (Something is missing here; so it is in the Mekhilta, Parashat Mishpatim.) Before teruma, which is called by only three names. Let teruma come before first tithe, for teruma is called by three names, reishit, teruma and dema, before first tithe, which is called by only two names. And let first tithe, which is called by two names, reishit and ma’aser, come before second tithe, which has no… Let teruma come before first tithe, for teruma is called by three names, teruma and ma’aser [so the text reads], before second tithe, which has only one name, ma’aser. And about them all it is written: “Your fullness and your outflow you shall not delay,” that one shall not put off what comes first; and it wrote a prohibition, for lashes.] [This note’s text is damaged and partly repeated.]
rashi:a5.1: The tithe of this one is in that one: the tithe I must separate from this basket shall be in that basket, so that I take from this one for that one. Or if he said, “of this one in that one, and of that one in this one,” that I will separate from this basket for the other basket and from the other basket for this basket: the first is tithed, even though he did not separate at once, as we say about a barrel of wine, “[the two log] that I am going to separate” and so on: he deconsecrates and drinks at once, even though he did not separate from the barrel at once. All the more so here, where he deconsecrates and eats at once, since they are two vessels. But the second is not tithed, even when he said “of this one in that one and of that one in this one”: because as soon as he said “of this one in that one,” the first shall be tithe for the second, and at once the second is fully exempt [so the text reads]; and when he said “of this one,” that the second shall be tithe for the first, his words are nothing, since the second was already exempted through the first basket, and one may not separate from exempt produce for obligated produce.
tosafot:a5.1: If there were before him two baskets of untithed produce, and he said, “The tithe of this is in that,” the first is tithed: for example, if there are a hundred figs in each basket, ten of the second shall be first tithe for the first, and he also designates second tithe; all hundred of the first are then rectified. And it deals with demai, since he does not separate teruma, and it is taught in tractate Demai (7:6).
rashi:a6.1: And if he said: Their tithes are the tithe of each basket in its fellow: that is, these two tithes that I am going to separate from these two baskets, the tithes of each one shall be the tithe of the basket in its fellow, that is, each basket shall be exempted through its fellow basket, which is “of this one in that one and of that one in this one.”
rashi:a6.2: He has declared the name: so he may deconsecrate and eat at once from both, even though he has not yet separated anything. And here one cannot say “from exempt produce for obligated produce,” since both are rectified at once, with one utterance, so it is from obligated produce for obligated produce.
tosafot:a6.1: “Of this in that, and of that in this,” the first is tithed: for as soon as he said “of this in that,” it is rectified and becomes exempt. When he then says “and of that in this,” it turns out that he tithes from exempt produce for obligated produce, and it is nothing.
tosafot:a6.2: “Their tithes are the tithe of each basket in its fellow,” he has declared the name: for they are rectified together, each through the other. And even though we hold that whatever cannot take effect one after the other cannot take effect even at once, here, since his intention is to rectify both, it is like one who says: the tithe of the first shall be in the second, except for ten [figs] that shall remain untithed in the first to rectify the second. So the tithe of this in that and of that in this takes effect.
gershom:a7.1: And he said: The tithe of this shall be in that: the first is tithed. And likewise if he said, “The tithe of this in that, and of that in this,” the first is tithed but not the second. For when he separated from the second for the first, he separated from obligated produce for obligated produce; and if he now goes back and separates from the first for the second, [it turns out he separates] from exempt produce, already rectified, for obligated produce, and that is not teruma. But if he said: [All] the tithes of these two baskets shall be the tithe of each basket in its fellow, for example, he sets his eyes on one side of each to be tithe for its fellow, since their tithes were (divided) [rectified] at once, he has declared the name and they are tithed.
rashi:a7.1: Because he put the second tithe in it before the first tithe: for at the outset, before he said “of this one in that one,” it stood to have first tithe and second tithe separated from it. Now that he goes back and separates first tithe and second tithe from it for the other basket, the second tithe of this basket comes before the first tithe that he stood to separate from the other basket earlier. And likewise when he said “of this one in that one, and of that one in this one,” he puts the second tithe in it before the second tithe in its fellow [so the text reads] in the same way. And for this he is flogged, since a person must separate first tithe and second tithe in this order, as it is written: “Your fullness and your outflow you shall not delay.” Just as he is warned not to hold back the fullness for the mixture, so he is warned not to hold back first tithe for second tithe, as it is written “and your outflow you shall not delay”: whatever is included in “mixture” is under “you shall not delay,” that is, whatever carries the status of teruma [as first tithe carries terumat ma’aser] is under “you shall not delay,” so that he separates first tithe and then second tithe; and if he put second tithe before first tithe, he transgresses “you shall not delay.” Another version: we expound in the Mekhilta: Let first fruits come before teruma, because first fruits are more stringent, having four names: reishit, mele’a, teruma and bikkurim; while teruma has only three names: reishit, dema and teruma. And let teruma come before first tithe, which has only two names, ma’aser and terumat ma’aser. And let first tithe, which has two names, also come before second tithe, which has only one name, second tithe. The verse says “your fullness and your outflow,” for it speaks of all of them: the most stringent among them shall not be put off, but one puts the stringent before the lenient. And just as Rabbi Elazar said that one who puts second tithe before first tithe is flogged, so too he says it of one who puts teruma before first fruits.
tosafot:a7.1: And it was stated about it: Rabbi Elazar says he is flogged, because he put the second tithe in it before the first tithe in its fellow: for the first and second tithes of the first basket are as if separated, while the first tithe of the second is still untithed within it. This refers to the first clause, where he said “the tithe of this in that,” [and the first is] tithed. And in the Jerusalem Talmud we read: “For the first by a positive mitzva, and for the second by a prohibition.” One may explain: for the first, if he fixed their tithes within it, he transgresses a positive mitzva, since he should have put first tithe before second, yet he declared their names at once; but there is no prohibition, since he did not put second before first. And for the second, by a prohibition: when he rectified the first within it, for he put the second tithe of the first before the first tithe of the second. Some read it the other way: “For the first by a prohibition, and for the second by a positive mitzva,” and this is the meaning: on the first clause of the mishna, when he said “the tithe of this in that,” he transgresses a prohibition, since he puts second tithe before first, as I explained; and on the second, that is, on the last clause of the mishna, when he said “their tithes are the tithe of each basket in its fellow,” there is no prohibition but only a positive mitzva, since they are at once.
tosafot:a7.2: Because he put the second tithe in it before the first tithe in its fellow: even though the verse speaks only of first fruits and teruma, it is also explained of first tithe after teruma and second tithe after first tithe, since it is written: “and your outflow you shall not delay”: whatever is included in “mixture,” you shall not delay. The reason is explained in the Mishna (Terumot 3:7): First fruits come before teruma because they are called [both] first fruits and teruma; teruma before first tithe because it is called teruma and reishit; and first tithe before second, because it contains reishit, meaning it contains terumat ma’aser. The Mekhilta gives another reason, and Rashi wrote, in his words: Let first fruits come before teruma because they have four names, reishit, mele’a, teruma and bikkurim, while teruma has only three names, reishit, dema and teruma; let teruma come before first tithe, which has only two names, ma’aser and terumat ma’aser; and let first tithe come before second, which has only one name, second tithe. The verse says “your fullness and your outflow you shall not delay,” for it speaks of all of them: the most stringent of them you shall not put off, but put the stringent before the lenient. And just as Rabbi Elazar says one is flogged for putting second tithe before first, so too for putting first tithe before teruma and teruma before first fruits. End of his words.
gershom:a8.1: And it was stated about it: Rabbi Elazar said he is flogged. This refers to the first clause: even though we say the first is tithed, he is flogged, because when he said “the tithe of this in that,” it implies [all the tithes of this in that, so he has put] the second tithe in it before he separates the first tithe of its fellow; and a person may not separate second tithe until he has separated first tithe from each basket, for we said above that “you shall not delay” [applies] to all of them. [If so, the first statement is difficult: what we said in the name of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina, that they said, “Also one who separates teruma before first fruits.” No: when the statement of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina was said, he was referring to the exemption, “one is not flogged,” and this is what he says, and so on.]
rashi:b1.1: And it answers: he was referring to the exemption. So there is no difficulty from Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina against Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina; Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina comes to say that also one who declares the name of teruma before first fruits transgresses a prohibition with no action, and he is not flogged.
rashi:b2.1: And what is different about one who effects substitution, that he is flogged: as you said above, “except for one who takes an oath and one who effects substitution.”
rashi:b2.2: If we say because with his speech: that he says “this in place of this,” he performs an action, for at first it was non-sacred and now it is sacred.
rashi:b2.3: This is the reading: One who puts teruma before first fruits also performs an action with his speech, for he declares its name and brings it into the sanctity of teruma.
rashi:b3.1: A prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva: the prohibition, as it is written (Exodus 22:28): “Your fullness and your outflow you shall not delay”; the positive mitzva, as it is written (Numbers 18:28): “From all your tithes you shall set apart.” This is expounded elsewhere, and in the discussion below (Temurah 5b), as tithe that he separated first while the grain was in the heap: he transgressed the prohibition “you shall not delay” by putting tithe before teruma, and the verse detached the prohibition from lashes, and they established it as a case where he goes back and separates [the teruma]. And even though they are not written next to each other, it is counted as a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva, and therefore he is not flogged.
gershom:b1.1: Rectified it by a positive mitzva, as it is written: “From all your tithes you shall set apart,” to say that one is not flogged for it if he put [it] first.
gershom:b2.1: And he was saying this teaching: that for this reason he is not flogged, since the verse rectified it by a positive mitzva.
tosafot:b4.1: In brief: Could Abaye really have thought that one is flogged for a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva? There is an explicit mishna (Ḥullin 141b) that one who took the mother bird with the young sends her away and is not flogged, because it is a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva; for notar too the baraita says the verse put a positive mitzva after the prohibition so that one is not flogged; and we learned that a rapist who divorced remarries and is not flogged. The Ri answers: in the mother bird, notar and the rapist, the positive mitzva is written right next to the prohibition, and there Abaye took it as obvious that one is not flogged. What surprised him was the prohibition about tithes, where “from all your tithes you shall set apart” is not next to “you shall not delay.” He objected from substitution, even though there the positive mitzva is next to the prohibition, by comparing one case to another: just as one is flogged for substitution, though its prohibition is rectified by a positive mitzva, because he does not fulfill the positive mitzva with his own hands, so “from all your tithes,” though he fulfills it with his own hands, should not count as rectifying, since it is not next to the prohibition. Restoring a stolen item (Leviticus 5:23) is not next to its prohibition either, yet it is a full rectification, since restoring is possible only after the prohibition was transgressed; but “from all your tithes” can be fulfilled even when the prohibition was not transgressed. Even so, Abaye compared it to substitution. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b5.1: But one who effects substitution, which is a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva: the prohibition, as it is written (Leviticus 27:10): “He shall not exchange it”; the positive mitzva: “and if he shall at all change.”
rashi:b6.1: Two prohibitions and a positive mitzva: “He shall not exchange it” and “nor substitute it”; and therefore he incurs the forty lashes.
gershom:b3.1: Two prohibitions: “He shall not exchange it” and “nor substitute it”; and one positive mitzva: “and if he shall at all change.”
gershom:b8.1: Another version: Substitution is different, and that is why the positive mitzva does not cancel the prohibition: it is a prohibition that applies equally to all, since everyone is forbidden to substitute at the outset, while its positive mitzva, “and if he shall at all change,” does not apply equally to all, since it does not apply to the community or to partners, who cannot effect substitution even after the fact. Therefore the positive mitzva is not strong enough to override a prohibition that applies equally to all.
rashi:b7.1: But there is the rapist: one who rapes a virgin, for so it is written in that passage: “He may not send her away” [Deuteronomy 22:29].
rashi:b7.2: And one positive mitzva: as it is written there: “And she shall be his wife.”
rashi:b7.3: If he is an Israelite, he remarries: because he stands under “arise and remarry,” and he can fulfill both the positive mitzva and the prohibition, since remarriage is possible. But a priest, who does not stand under “arise and remarry,” since he may not marry his divorcée, is certainly flogged for “he may not send her away all his days.” For the positive mitzva does not come and uproot the prohibition to say that he is not flogged; he is certainly flogged. And this is difficult for the one who says that one is not flogged for a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva.
gershom:b4.1: The rapist, who has one prohibition and one positive mitzva: the positive mitzva is “and she shall be his wife”; the prohibition, as it is written: “He may not send her away.”
tosafot:b7.1: But there is the rapist, with one prohibition and one positive mitzva, and the one positive mitzva does not come and uproot the prohibition: that is, according to you, who said that “from all your tithes you shall set apart” speaks only of the order of teruma and tithe, and even so it rectifies [breaking] the order of first fruits and tithe [so the text reads], evidently you hold that where a prohibition is rectified in part, we say it is rectified entirely. But there is the rapist, whose prohibition is rectified for an Israelite, and we do not say it is rectified for a priest. Evidently where part is rectified, the whole is not rectified.
gershom:b5.1: And if he is a priest, he is flogged: since he transgressed the prohibition “he may not send her away.”
gershom:b6.1: And does not remarry: since he is forbidden to a divorcée. Evidently the positive mitzva does not help a priest escape lashes.
rashi:b8.1: This is the reading: Priests are different, for that is another reason: the verse gave them added holiness, as it is written: “Speak to the priests… none shall become impure for the dead” [Leviticus 21:1]. Since their holiness is more stringent, the Torah was stricter with them than with Israelites, so that they are flogged even for a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva, though an Israelite is not flogged. Another version: when he objected, “But there is one who effects substitution,” the answer was: it is different there, and that is why he is flogged, because substitution is a prohibition that applies equally to all, since everyone is forbidden to substitute. Then he objects: “But there is the rapist,” and so on, where his prohibition, “he may not send her away,” does not apply equally to all but only to an Israelite: if an Israelite divorced her, he can then fulfill the prohibition; but a priest who divorced does not remarry and cannot fulfill the prohibition, and even so the priest is flogged, as it teaches: “He is flogged and does not remarry.” Why? Let us say: since his prohibition is weak, not applying equally to all, this priest should not be flogged, for the positive mitzva, strong enough to apply equally to all, should uproot it. And it answers: priests are another reason, and that is why we are strict with them that they are flogged, even though it is not a prohibition that applies equally to all. But for Israelites, where the prohibition and the positive mitzva apply equally to all, that is, to all Israelites, who all stand under “arise and remarry,” he is not flogged, since it is a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva.
tosafot:b8.1: You say priests? Priests are different, for the Merciful One gave them extra holiness: Rashi explained that for this reason the Torah was strict, that they are flogged even though it is a prohibition that does not apply equally to all. This is not convincing. The Ri explained: since the verse forbade a divorcée to them, the prohibition is not rectified by the positive mitzva. This is unlike the case above, where it said that “you shall set apart” rectifies also putting [teruma] before first fruits, from which we learn that he can repair it if he did wrong and put teruma before first fruits; for it is all the same whether he put tithe before teruma or teruma before first fruits.
gershom:b7.1: That is why he is flogged: because the Merciful One gave priests extra holiness. But elsewhere, for a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva, one is not flogged.
gershom:b9.1: But there is the rapist, whose prohibition does not apply equally to all, since it does not apply to priests: for we do not say of a priest, “he may not send her away all his days,” as though, if he divorced her, all his days he stands under “arise and remarry,” as an Israelite is obligated; rather, once he has divorced her, he does not take her back. And his positive mitzva, “and she shall be his wife, because he has violated her,” applies equally to all, even to priests; and even so the positive mitzva is not strong enough to exempt priests from lashes. He said to him: Priests are another reason, so the Torah was strict with them that they are flogged. But for Israelites, where the prohibition applies equally to all and the positive mitzva applies equally to all, the positive mitzva comes and removes him from the prohibition, and he is not flogged; rather, he remarries and is not flogged, since the verse rectified it by a positive mitzva, as Rabbi Avin said.
tosafot:b9.1: It is subject to a dispute between tanna’im: this does not refer to this discussion of a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva, but to the dispute about a prohibition that involves no action.
rashi:b9.1: To place a positive mitzva: “but that which remains of it” after the prohibition, so it is a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva.
rashi:b10.1: A prohibition that involves no action: for when he leaves it over, he performs no action.
rashi:b11.1: And Rabbi Ya’akov: who said “it is not for that reason,” and so on. This “but that which remains of it,” what does he do with it, since he does not need it for a prohibition rectified by a positive mitzva?
tosafot:b11.1: And Rabbi Ya’akov, what does he do with “but that which remains”? And if you say: it is needed to teach us the law of burning! One may say that he asks from its placement: for what halakha did the Torah write it here, next to the prohibition? If it does not come to rectify the prohibition, let it be written elsewhere.
rashi:b12.1: For that which we learned: in tractate Pesaḥim, in the chapter Keitzad Tzolin (Pesaḥim 83a).
rashi:b12.2: They are burned on the sixteenth: and not on the fifteenth, which is a Festival day, and consecrated meat is not burned on a Festival day.
gershom:b10.1: The bones and the sinews: of the Paschal offering.
gershom:b11.1: They are burned on the sixteenth: because burning overrides neither Shabbat nor a Festival day.
rashi:b13.1: What is the reason? The verse states “but that which remains of it” and so on, a second morning, that is, the sixteenth. For so the verse implies: “you shall let nothing of it remain until morning,” that is, until the morning of the fifteenth; and if some of it remains until the next morning, “you shall burn with fire,” that is, on the sixteenth, which is the intermediate days of the Festival.
gershom:b12.1: And Ḥizkiyya said, and so on.
rashi:b14.2: It is effective: what he did is done, since he is flogged.
rashi:b14.3: It is not effective: as is explained below.
rashi:b14.4: This is the reading: “And this, that he is flogged, is because he transgressed,” and so on.
gershom:b13.1: If he does it, it is effective: that is, even though he transgressed, what he did is done. For if it were not effective, he has done nothing, so why is he flogged?
tosafot:b14.1: Rava said: It is not effective at all. This is difficult: if so, one who slaughters the Paschal offering while leaven is in his possession should disqualify it! One may say that in the Jerusalem Talmud there is a verse that validates it. And it is difficult: one who slits the ear of a firstborn should make it forbidden [since, on Rava’s view, the forbidden blemish should not count], yet it is obvious to us that it is forbidden only as a penalty. One may say: it is no worse than if a blemish had befallen it by itself, which is permitted. And from this it is settled why one who slits an ear does not make it forbidden under “anything I have made abominable to you is under ‘do not eat,’” as with meat in milk: only meat in milk is derived from that, since even if the meat fell into the milk by itself it is forbidden; but slitting an ear, which is permitted when it happens by itself, is not under “do not eat” even when done by hand. This requires further study.
